title: Loner Kids May Be Happier Than You Think
gist: A University of Georgia study of over 470 fourth- and fifth-graders, published in The Elementary School Journal, examines whether children who prefer to play alone despite getting along with peers are less happy, using peer nominations plus self-reported friendship quality and belonging.

insights.claim: New research suggests that children who prefer to play alone during a crucial developmental period are not necessarily headed for unhappiness.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Challenges the common assumption that a preference for solitary play in childhood is inherently a warning sign.
insights.quote: New research published in The Elementary School Journal is offering a glimpse into the interior lives of schoolchildren, and the good news is that playing solo isn’t necessarily a prelude to unhappiness.

insights.claim: Psychologists from the University of Georgia asked more than 470 fourth- and fifth-graders to identify fellow students who preferred to play alone despite getting along well with others.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Describes the peer-nomination method used to identify voluntarily solitary children, distinguishing them from socially rejected children.
insights.quote: Psychologists from the University of Georgia asked more than 470 fourth- and fifth-graders to list fellow students who preferred to play alone, despite getting along well with others.

insights.claim: Students were also asked to report on the quality of their own one-on-one friendships and how they felt about belonging to a larger peer group.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Shows the study measured both dyadic friendship quality and group-belonging separately, allowing a more nuanced picture of solitary children's social well-being.
